planting.note: Repot in spring into a container only slightly larger than the rootball, since this compact selection resents being overpotted.

directions: This selection keeps the same bold, violin-shaped leaves as the standard fiddle-leaf fig but on a shorter, denser, more multi-branched frame, making it easier to fit into an average living room. Place near an east- or south-facing window with bright, filtered light and rotate the pot occasionally so growth stays even on all sides. Water only when the top two inches of soil have dried out, since both soggy roots and prolonged drought cause the same brown-edged leaf drop this species is known for. Wipe the leaves periodically to remove dust and keep them photosynthesizing efficiently, and hold off on fertilizer during the darker winter months.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ficus lyrata
American Society for Horticultural Science houseplant guides

planting.note: Give this variegated selection more light than a plain-green fiddle-leaf fig to keep the cream leaf margins from fading to solid green.

directions: The large, glossy, violin-shaped leaves of this cultivar are edged and marbled in cream to pale yellow, so it needs noticeably brighter indirect light than green-leaved forms to hold its pattern without scorching. Because it carries less chlorophyll than an all-green fiddle-leaf, growth is slower and it is more sensitive to both underwatering and waterlogged soil, so let the top few inches of mix dry before rewatering. Any all-green reversion shoots should be pruned out promptly, since they grow faster and will eventually overtake the variegated growth if left in place. Keep away from cold drafts and heating vents, both of which cause rapid leaf drop in this species.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Ficus lyrata
Royal Horticultural Society houseplant care notes

planting.note: This vigorous cultivar is the classic thick-leaved rubber plant sold at most nurseries; repot every one to two years as roots fill the container.

directions: Robusta is the standard, extra-vigorous rubber tree cultivar prized for its very large, thick, glossy dark-green leaves and fast upright growth. Grow it in bright, indirect light, since low light causes long, sparse internodes and smaller leaves, and rotate the plant periodically to keep growth balanced around a strong central cane. Allow the top half of the soil to dry between waterings and reduce frequency in winter, as this cultivar is notably intolerant of soggy, poorly drained potting mix. Wipe down the broad leaves regularly, both to keep the plant looking its best and because dust buildup reduces light capture on such large leaf surfaces.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ficus elastica
Iowa State University Extension houseplant guides

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring when repotting, ensuring each division keeps healthy roots and at least a few leaves.

directions: This striking cultivar layers dark green, cream, and rose-pink streaks along the top of each oval leaf, with deep maroon undersides that show off as the leaves fold up at night in typical prayer-plant fashion. Provide bright, indirect light out of direct sun, which quickly scorches the thin, patterned foliage, and keep humidity high with regular misting or a pebble tray to prevent crispy leaf edges. Water enough to keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, and use filtered or rain water when possible since this species is sensitive to the fluoride and salts in some tap water. Feed lightly during the growing season and repot every year or two as it is a fairly fast, clump-forming grower.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ctenanthe oppenheimiana

planting.note: Divide offsets from the base in spring or early summer when repotting into fresh, well-drained mix.

directions: Emerald Beauty produces lance-shaped, deep green leaves brushed with irregular silvery-gray flecking, giving it a mottled, almost hand-painted look that stands out against plainer greenhouse foliage. It tolerates low light better than most houseplants, making it well suited to interior offices and rooms with only a north-facing window, though it grows fuller with bright indirect light. Let the top inch or two of potting mix dry before watering again, since this species is more prone to root rot from overwatering than to any drought stress. Keep it away from cold drafts and temperatures below about 60 degrees Fahrenheit, and wear gloves when handling cut stems because the sap can irritate skin.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Repot and divide in spring, using a fast-draining aroid mix to reduce the risk of stem rot.

directions: Sparkling Sarah is a compact, colorful cultivar with pink-blushed stems and leaves speckled in cream, pink, and green, prized for adding warm color to shaded interior plantings without needing flowers. Bright, indirect light brings out the pink coloring most strongly, while deep shade causes the foliage to green up and lose contrast. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, keeping the plant on the slightly drier side in winter when growth slows, and provide warmth and humidity above 60 percent for the best leaf color. Because it stays small and dense, it works well in tabletop displays or grouped dish gardens rather than as a floor specimen.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production guide
